title: Khronos NegativeScaleTest -- a negative determinant reverses a primitive's winding, which back-face culling has to follow or a whole plate goes missing

criterion.says: This model tests what happens when a glTF node has negative scaling, such that the mesh it contains is inverted, and the vertex winding order swaps from counter-clockwise to clockwise. ... This means that when a mesh flips inside-out due to its hierarchy of transforms, the winding order is expected to become reversed (clockwise instead of counterclockwise), and features such as back-face culling and lighting need to account for this change. ... PROBLEM: Negative Scale with Back-Face Culling ... In the above image, the renderer has not properly accounted for a negative scale, resulting in back-face culling being inappropriately applied to negatively-scaled meshes. In the second row, the front face (clockwise due to negative scale) should be shown, and the back face (counter-clockwise) should be culled.
criterion.note: THE ASSET STATES TWO PROBLEMS AND THIS CASE DECIDES ONE OF THEM. Khronos's first is culling under a reversed winding, and that is a question about WHICH PIXELS ARE COVERED: `ChecksAndXMaterial` declares no `doubleSided`, so the format's default false applies and a renderer that ignores the determinant culls the front of the negatively-scaled plate and draws nothing where a plate belongs. That is a whole rectangle present or absent, not a tie at an edge. Khronos's second is the normal vectors -- `the two white spheres should be lit the same, regardless of the negative scaling on one of them` -- and an emitter gathers nothing, so no emission render can decide it. It is settled instead where it is decidable without a light at all: `test/unit/gltf/ANegativeDeterminantNeedsNoSecondNormalFlip.cpp` reads this same pinned asset and checks the geometric normal of every re-wound triangle against its own attribute normals and against the sphere it came from. Two halves, two instruments, one asset, and neither is a repair of the other.

acceptanceClass.because: A fronto-parallel planar placement owns three continuous freedoms -- two of aim and one of scale -- and every distinct silhouette line costs one condition, so 2 + k >= E is what decides whether the construction can be written at all (`board/`). Khronos's NegativeScaleTest is fourteen parts and 7 724 triangles, and its projected silhouette resolves into over four hundred distinct lines -- E is two orders above the freedoms, so the construction cannot be written for this subject at any camera. Its 495 disagreeing pixels are therefore NOT unconstructed placement: they sit on straight edges rather than on sphere rims and they exceed the oracle's own filter half-width by two orders, so they are a real disagreement and the case is red on the general-position bound.

subjects.name: NegativeScaleTest
subjects.notes: Eight root nodes over eight meshes and six materials. Node 4 `NegativeScaleFront` carries `scale [-1, -1, -1.0000001]` under a 180-degree rotation about Y, so its global determinant is negative and its plate is the one the culling question is about; nodes 10 and 13 put a negative scale on a PARENT, so their children inherit a reversed winding without carrying a negative scale themselves -- which is why the specification states the rule over the GLOBAL transform and why a reader that looked at the node's own TRS would pass three of these and fail three. The texture sets are not read: the two textured materials are replaced below, because what this case decides is which faces survive culling and a sampler in the path would put a second disagreement into a comparison about the first.

source.pinReason: the same pin every other Khronos subject in this tree carries

blender.note: A release version, not a commit. Recorded so a red rung can be attributed to our renderer or to the oracle, and carried in the oracle's cache key so a version bump misses instead of serving a stale render. We do not aim to be bit-identical with Cycles.

camera.derivation: The framing rule of board:0083 (src/gltf/Framing.h) applied to this subject's own bounds and to nothing else, and the numbers are the instrument's own output rather than a second evaluation of the same arithmetic: test/unit/gltf/ADerivedCameraIsTheFramingRuleAndNotAQuotation prints the rule's eye, aim, lens and clip range for every case it walks, and this camera is that line. THE ROLL IS ZERO AND STATED, and this camera carries NEITHER exactness condition of `board/` -- no rational roll and no lattice offset. It is therefore an unconstructed placement of exactly the class the 2026-08-13 ruling holds red, and it is recorded as such rather than as a subject that cannot be constructed: the freedoms are ours, the silhouette that disagrees is straight, and whether the count 2 + k >= E is met is a question for the round that constructs.
camera.note: THE ENGINE'S OWN ANSWER, QUOTED (board:1398). Every number here is read from the framing rule's output for this subject -- eye, aim, yfov and both clip planes -- rather than recomputed by the authoring helper, which bounded each primitive by the eight transformed corners of its local AABB and therefore always at least as loosely as the engine bounds the transformed vertices. A looser radius moves the eye back, and 93 cases declared a camera the rule does not derive. `ADerivedCameraIsTheFramingRuleAndNotAQuotation` recomputes all of it and refuses a mismatch, so what this declaration does is PIN the viewpoint, never choose it.

light.note: An emitter gathers nothing, so there is nothing for a light to do here. The half of Khronos's criterion that needs one is the normals half, and it is decided by test/unit/gltf/ANegativeDeterminantNeedsNoSecondNormalFlip.cpp against the geometry itself rather than against a render.

world.note: BLACK, AND THAT IS THE REDUCTION RATHER THAN A LOOK. This subject occludes itself -- plates stand in front of a background quad and spheres in front of both -- and Cycles at one sample against the factory world is a Bernoulli draw on the visible sky fraction, which is an ambient-occlusion estimator wearing a placement's clothes (board:0087). With the world at zero and every closure an emitter there is no integral left, so the two seeds must agree bit for bit and a difference between them NAMES what survived.

material.note: ONE COLOUR PER MATERIAL, which is the key a multi-material asset has. Four of the six are the file's own baseColorFactor verbatim, so they are recomputable from the pinned asset. TWO ARE NOT AND EACH SAYS WHY: `ChecksAndXMaterial` and `LabelMat` carry a baseColorTexture and no factor, so the format's default [1,1,1,1] is what the file states for them -- `ChecksAndXMaterial` takes that default unchanged, and `LabelMat` is set to 0.5 grey [SET] so the label strip and the check plates do not fuse into one white region that no coverage metric can tell apart. `So Shiny` is halved from its own 0.8 [SET] for the same reason against `Not So Shiny`, which is the sphere pair the second half of the criterion is about. Neither substitution touches the question: what this case decides is WHICH FACES SURVIVE CULLING, and a face that is culled is absent at any colour.

default.note: One sample per pixel with the box filter at its RNA minimum makes Cycles evaluate the same predicate a centre-sampling rasteriser does, because the integer raster coordinate is the pixel centre and the sample never leaves +/-0.005 px of it.

seed-shift.note: The same recipe at another seed, and the whole of the emission case's acceptance. A Monte-Carlo estimator's answer depends on its seed; an emitter under a black world has no estimator, so the two dumps must agree bit for bit and any difference NAMES the integral that survived.

notes: The first case in this tree whose verdict turns on a face being culled. Every earlier coverage case is winding-blind by construction -- a closed convex body keeps its silhouette under a global flip, and an open one drawn double-sided keeps it too -- so nothing until now could tell a renderer that reads the determinant from one that ignores it. This asset's plates are open, single-sided and half of them inside-out, which makes the answer a rectangle rather than a pixel.

subjectFrameFraction.note: The fraction of the frame the subject's projected area covers at frame 0, RE-HARVESTED after the camera became the framing rule's own answer (board:1398). Recomputed by the runner on every run and refused on mismatch, so this line PINS the framing and never chooses it; seeded from that recomputation, it is a drift detector rather than a present-error check.
